# 1 Samuel Chapter 19 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 181r-181v | **Source Image:** 1SA_019_page_001.jpg, 1SA_019_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan, Saul's son, was deeply devoted to David.

**2** Jonathan warned David, "My father Saul is trying to kill you. Be on your guard tomorrow morning. Go into hiding and stay in a secret place.

**3** I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are hiding. I will speak to my father about you, and if I learn anything, I will tell you."

**4** Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul. He said to him, "Let the king not sin against his servant David, because he has not sinned against you. On the contrary, his deeds have been of great benefit to you.

**5** He took his life in his hands when he struck down the Philistine, and the LORD won a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and rejoiced. Why then would you sin against innocent blood by killing David for no reason?"

**6** Saul listened to Jonathan's voice and swore an oath: "As the LORD lives, David will not be put to death."

**7** Jonathan called David and told him all these things. Jonathan brought David to Saul, and David was in his presence as before.

**8** When war broke out again, David went out and fought the Philistines. He struck them with such force that they fled before him.

**9** Then a tormenting spirit from the LORD came upon Saul as he sat in his house with his spear in his hand, while David was playing the lyre.

**10** Saul tried to pin David to the wall with the spear, but David slipped away from Saul's thrust, and the spear struck the wall. David fled and escaped that night.

**11** Saul sent men to David's house to watch it and to kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, warned him, "If you do not save yourself tonight, tomorrow you will be dead."

**12** So Michal lowered David through a window, and he fled and escaped.

**13** Then Michal took the household idol, laid it on the bed, put a covering of goat's hair at its head, and covered it with a garment.

**14** When Saul sent men to capture David, she said, "He is ill."

**15** Saul sent the men back to see David, telling them, "Bring him up to me on his bed so I can kill him."

**16** When the men entered, there was the idol on the bed with the goat's hair at its head.

**17** Saul said to Michal, "Why did you deceive me like this and let my enemy escape?" Michal answered Saul, "He said to me, 'Let me go! Why should I have to kill you?'"

**18** When David had fled and escaped, he went to Samuel at Ramah and told him everything Saul had done to him. Then he and Samuel went and stayed at Naioth.

**19** Saul was told, "David is at Naioth in Ramah."

**20** So Saul sent men to capture David. But when they saw the company of prophets prophesying with Samuel standing as their leader, the Spirit of God came upon Saul's men and they also began to prophesy.

**21** When Saul was told about this, he sent more men, and they also prophesied. Saul sent men a third time, and they too prophesied.

**22** Then Saul himself went to Ramah. When he came to the great cistern at Secu, he asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" Someone said, "They are at Naioth in Ramah."

**23** So Saul went to Naioth in Ramah. But the Spirit of God came upon him also, and he walked along prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah.

**24** He stripped off his garments and he too prophesied in Samuel's presence. He lay there naked all that day and all that night. That is why people say, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

- **19:4 — "He took his life in his hands"**: The Hebrew idiom *va-yasem et-naphsho v'khappo* (וַיָּשֶׂם אֶת־נַפְשׁוֹ בְכַפּוֹ) means literally "he placed his soul in his palm" — holding his own life as something expendable. Jonathan's defense of David before Saul is legally structured, presenting evidence of David's loyalty and benefit to the crown. The son advocates for the man who will replace his father.

- **19:13 — "The household idol" (teraphim)**: The Hebrew *teraphim* (תְּרָפִים) reveals a startling detail — David's household contained an idol large enough to simulate a sleeping man. The narrator does not comment or condemn. Michal's use of the teraphim is practical deception, not worship, but its presence in David's house reflects the religious complexity of the period. The goat-hair pillow (*k'vir ha-izzim*) was likely woven fabric, arranged to look like hair.

- **19:20-24 — The contagion of prophetic ecstasy**: Three successive groups of soldiers and then Saul himself are overwhelmed by the Spirit when they enter Samuel's prophetic community at Naioth. The verb *va-yitnab'u* (וַיִּתְנַבְּאוּ — "they prophesied") in the hithpael stem suggests ecstatic, involuntary behavior. The Spirit of God functions here as divine protection for David — it incapacitates every pursuer, turning warriors into worshippers.

- **19:24 — "Is Saul also among the prophets?"**: This proverb appears twice in 1 Samuel (cf. 10:12), but with drastically different valences. In chapter 10, Saul's prophesying at the beginning of his reign was a sign of divine empowerment. Here at the end, the same phenomenon is a sign of divine judgment — he lies stripped and helpless, unable even to pursue his quarry. The same Spirit that once elevated Saul now humiliates him.

- **19:11-12 — Michal's window**: Michal's lowering of David through the window echoes Rahab's rescue of the Israelite spies (Joshua 2:15). Both are acts of subversive loyalty by women within enemy-controlled spaces — choosing covenant allegiance over household authority. The wife of the failed king protects the future king.

— *PNEUMA*
